items.prompt: At Otjiwarongo Beverages there are six levels of management between the managing director and the shop floor. Explain why decisions in such a tall structure tend to take longer to reach the workers who must carry them out.
items.canonical_answer: In a tall structure each decision passes along the chain of command through every level between the managing director and the shop floor, because each level must receive the instruction, understand it and pass it on. Six levels therefore means six stages of passing on before the first worker sees the decision, and each stage adds waiting and discussion time. As the instruction travels, each level can also filter or reword it, so the message that finally arrives may differ from the one that was sent - a further reason decisions are not just slower but less reliable by the time they arrive.
marking_guidance: Reason: award for the chain of command forcing the decision through every level, because each level must relay it before it moves on. Second reason: award for filtering or distortion of the message as it travels down, which is why the decision that arrives can differ from the one that was sent.

items.prompt: Explain the features that separate a tall organisational structure from a short one.
items.canonical_answer: The features that tell them apart are: the number of levels of hierarchy - a tall structure has many levels, a short one has few; the span of control - tall structures have narrow spans, with each manager supervising a small number of subordinates, while short structures have wide spans; and the speed of decisions, because in a tall structure instructions pass through more levels of the chain of command, so they tend to arrive later than in a short one, where fewer levels stand between the top and the people doing the work.
marking_guidance: Features: award one mark for each element stated - many against few levels, narrow against wide spans of control, and the difference in decision speed - and one mark for developing each element into what it includes in practice.

items.prompt: The production supervisor at a steelworks in Otavi reports to the operations manager, who answers to a director. Explain why the responsibilities of the supervisor differ from those of the director in this business.
items.canonical_answer: The supervisor oversees day-to-day work at the first level above the operatives: shift rosters, machine problems, instructions to the workers on the floor, because his responsibility is today's output. The director sets the overall direction of the company - which products to make, whether to invest in a new furnace - and answers to the shareholders for the results, because her responsibility is the long-term performance of the whole business. The two roles differ because each answers to a different level of the hierarchy: the supervisor is accountable to the operations manager for daily performance, while the director is accountable to the owners for the strategy, and accountability is what shapes what each role must do.
marking_guidance: Reason: award for the time horizon of each role - daily output against long-term direction - because each answers to a different level. Second reason: award for accountability running to different people, the manager against the shareholders, which is why the responsibilities cannot be the same.

items.prompt: Explain the features of the inter-relationships between directors, managers, supervisors and other employees in an organisation.
items.canonical_answer: The features of the inter-relationships are: authority flowing downward, because directors set objectives that managers turn into departmental targets and supervisors turn into daily instructions for other employees; accountability flowing upward, because information about results travels back up the same chain, letting each level check the one below; and mutual dependence, because no level can do its job without the others - directors depend on supervisors' reports to know whether strategy is working, and other employees depend on supervisors for the instructions that make the work meaningful.

items.prompt: Explain why planning is usually the first of the management functions to be carried out.
items.canonical_answer: The other functions all need a plan to work on: organising has nothing to arrange people towards until objectives and a method have been fixed, and coordinating needs to know which parts must fit together and why. Commanding is empty without something to instruct staff to achieve, and controlling has no target to check results against until the plan sets one. Planning comes first, then, because every later function uses the plan as its starting point - a manager who skips it spends the rest of the week reacting to problems the plan would have prevented.
marking_guidance: Reason: award for the other functions depending on a plan to organise towards and command staff to achieve, because the plan is their starting point. Second reason: award for controlling needing the plan's targets as the measure for checking results.

items.prompt: Explain the difference between trusting a subordinate with a delegated task and keeping control over how it is done.
items.canonical_answer: Trust and control are the two faces of delegation, and the boundary between them is who decides the method. Trust gives the subordinate freedom over how the work is done: the manager hands over the task and lets the subordinate choose the approach. Control keeps the manager's check on progress and quality: agreed checkpoints, review of the finished work, a limit on what the subordinate may decide alone. Both sides matter, because delegation with no control leaves the manager unaware of problems, whereas control pressed so tight that every step needs approval is no longer delegation - the subordinate is merely doing as told. Effective delegation balances the two against the subordinate's experience and the importance of the task.
marking_guidance: Boundary: award for the distinction over who decides the method - the subordinate under trust, the manager under control. Both sides: award for showing each extreme failing - unchecked delegation hides problems, whereas total control removes the freedom that distinguishes delegation - and for the balance depending on experience and importance.

items.prompt: A depot manager delegates weekly stock ordering to a storeman but keeps no record of what is ordered and reviews nothing. If a manager delegates a task and monitors nothing about it, explain how problems could develop for the business.

items.prompt: Explain the features of effective delegation.
items.canonical_answer: Effective delegation has these features: a clearly defined task, so the subordinate knows exactly what is being handed over; authority matched to the task, because a subordinate told to schedule without the power to change rosters has been given a task without the means; a subordinate whose skills fit the work, since delegation assumes ability that must actually be there; an agreed check, such as a deadline or a review, that keeps the manager's control without smothering the subordinate; and retained accountability, because the manager remains answerable for the outcome. What the whole arrangement includes is trust in the method and control of the result - which is what lifts the manager's workload while developing the subordinate.
marking_guidance: Features: award one mark for each element - defined task, matched authority, fitted skills, an agreed check, retained accountability - and one mark for what the arrangement includes overall: trust in method with control of the result.

items.prompt: Explain why a democratic leadership style can raise motivation in a workplace.
items.canonical_answer: In a democratic style the leader consults the team and draws on its views before deciding, so staff feel their opinions count and are treated as people whose judgement matters. People usually commit more willingly to decisions they helped shape, because the decision is partly theirs, so they work to make it succeed rather than merely comply with it. Consultation also surfaces ideas from the people closest to the work - a guide knows the road conditions better than the owner - and seeing one's own suggestion adopted is itself motivating, which is why consulted staff tend to offer more ideas in the future as well.
marking_guidance: Reason: award for staff feeling their views count through consultation, because people commit more willingly to decisions they helped shape. Second reason: award for ideas from those closest to the work improving decisions, and adoption of a suggestion encouraging further contribution.

items.prompt: Explain the features of a laissez-faire leadership style.
items.canonical_answer: A laissez-faire style has these features: the leader sets few instructions, supplying broad goals rather than detailed orders; the team decides how to organise and carry out the work itself, including methods and division of tasks; the leader steps in rarely - mainly when asked, or when results slip; and the team is trusted to direct itself, which is why the style fits experienced, self-directed staff, as in a software studio of senior developers. What the style includes on the risk side: without the leader's supervision, the parts of the work can drift apart, and newer staff may be left without the direction they still need.
marking_guidance: Features: award one mark for each element - broad goals rather than orders, the team organising the work itself, the leader intervening rarely - and one mark for what the style includes on the cost side: weak coordination and unsupported new staff.

items.prompt: Tulia Interiors is a design studio in Windhoek with nine qualified interior designers. Its owner consults the team on every decision, from client briefs to paint suppliers. A corporate client has asked for a complete hotel lobby redesign, and the proposal must be with the client within 24 hours; the brief is detailed and the designers have all done similar hotel work before. Consider whether the owner should change her leadership style for this decision.
items.canonical_answer: Recommendation: keep the democratic style, but tighten it into one structured consultation followed by firm direction of the detail. The judgement rests on the context: the team's experience of hotel work is the studio's strongest asset for a hotel brief, so leaving that judgement unused would waste the very resource the 24 hours demand. The decisive criterion is the fit between team experience (high) and time available (short, but long enough for one working session): consultation is worth its cost here precisely because experienced designers will catch things in the brief that the owner alone would miss. The counterargument is real - a 24-hour deadline argues for an autocratic decision, with the owner simply assigning rooms, because consultation takes time, and an alternative route is to divide the lobby into sections and direct each designer immediately; but that saves an hour or two at the price of weaker designs and a signal to capable staff that their judgement is not wanted when it matters most. The recommendation depends on conditions: if the client's deadline moves closer or the brief changes materially, the owner should switch to autocratic task allocation for the remainder of the job; unless the team genuinely shares one view fast, a single session must replace open-ended consultation.
marking_guidance: Judgement: award for a clear recommendation - democratic in substance, tightened for time. Context: award for using the facts of this case - nine experienced designers, hotel experience, the detailed brief, the 24-hour deadline. Criterion: award for naming what decides it - team experience against the time available. Counterargument: award for the case against the recommendation, the autocratic alternative and what it saves and costs. Condition: award for the recommendation depending on stated conditions - a slipping deadline or a changed brief switching the choice.

items.prompt: A learner writes: "The manager of Rehoboth Hardware must have a democratic leadership style, because she has handed the daily cashing-up and banking to her senior cashier." Explain the error in this statement.
items.canonical_answer: The error is confusing delegation with democratic leadership. In fact they describe different things. Delegation is the passing of authority over a defined task to a named subordinate, while the manager remains answerable for the result. Democratic leadership is a leader's general way of reaching decisions: she consults the team and draws on its views before she decides. The test that tells them apart: ask whether authority over one specific task has moved to a named person, or whether the team's views were sought before a decision was made. Handing the cashing-up and banking to the senior cashier passes the first test, so it is delegation, but it does not show that anyone was consulted. The manager could have chosen the cashier and the task alone and simply announced it, which an autocratic leader is free to do. Her style would be democratic if she habitually asked her staff for their views before deciding - on opening hours or which suppliers to use, for example - and then took those views into account.
marking_guidance: The error is named and corrected: in fact handing a defined task to a named subordinate is delegation, which a leader of any style can do, while democratic leadership means consulting the team before deciding.

items.prompt: A learner writes: "The owner of Omaruru Leatherworks is an autocratic leader, because after hearing all ten craftworkers' ideas for the new handbag range, she made the final choice herself." Explain the mistake in this statement.
items.canonical_answer: The mistake is treating 'the leader made the final decision' as the mark of autocratic leadership. In fact autocratic and democratic leaders both keep the final decision; what separates the two styles is what happens before it. An autocratic leader decides alone and instructs staff what to do, without asking for their views. A democratic leader consults the team, draws on its views and then decides, so the decision is shaped by the people who do the work. The test that tells them apart: ask whether the team's views were sought and used before the decision was taken, not who announced it. The owner heard all ten craftworkers' ideas before choosing the range, so she consulted them, which is a democratic style. She would have been autocratic had she picked the range herself and simply told the workers what to make. And had the craftworkers chosen the range among themselves, the style would have been laissez-faire, not democratic.
marking_guidance: The error is named and corrected: in fact a democratic leader also takes the final decision; consulting the team first is what makes the style democratic rather than autocratic.

items.prompt: The managing director of Otjiwarongo Beverages wants to cut two of the six management levels between her office and the shop floor, and has asked for written advice. State two advantages and two disadvantages of removing the levels, each with a reason, and close with the way you would advise for this business.
items.canonical_answer: Advantages: decisions would travel a shorter chain of command, so instructions reach the shop floor faster and with less distortion, because fewer levels stand between the decision and the people carrying it out. Removing levels lowers the wage cost of management, because each level of managers is a cost the business can do without if spans can widen safely. Disadvantages: the remaining managers' spans of control widen, so supervision is less close and overload becomes a real risk, because one manager now watches what several watched before. The roles between the top and the shop floor are disturbed - supervisors and middle managers lose levels to report through or lose their posts - which can damage morale and the upward flow of information, because the chain that carried results back up is shortened abruptly. Advice for this business: remove one level at a time and check the effect on delivery and on the supervisors' workload before going further, since a six-level structure built around narrow spans needs retraining of the remaining managers to handle wider spans well.
marking_guidance: Point: award for each point stated, up to two per side. Reason: award for the because behind each point - fewer levels relay faster and distort less, wider spans overload, and so on. Context: award for applying each point to this bottling business - its six levels, its narrow spans - rather than arguing in the abstract.

items.prompt: Khorab Harvest Foods, a maize milling business near Otavi, employs 60 mill workers at N$14 an hour for 8 hours a day, 250 days a year. Until this year the owner set each worker's pay individually. All 60 workers have now joined the Namibian Food Workers Union, which asks for a rise of N$1 an hour and asks the owner to bargain with the union as the workers' single representative. The owner says he "does not discuss pay with outsiders". His operations manager, Selma, has good relations with the workforce and has offered to lead the talks. Using the figures, consider how the owner should respond to the union's request and who should lead the talks.
items.canonical_answer: The figures: the union's claim costs 60 x 1 x 8 x 250 = 120 000 a year, against a current wage bill of 60 x 14 x 8 x 250 = 1 680 000 - the claim adds about one fourteenth to the wage bill, which a milling business of this size can be expected to absorb in a normal year. Recommendation: the owner should recognise the union and bargain with it, and delegate the talks to Selma within limits he sets in advance. The judgement rests on the context: with all 60 workers unionised, there is no individual pay-setting left to defend - the workforce has already made itself collective, so refusing to bargain with it addresses a fact rather than preventing one. The decisive criterion is the strength of the combined workforce against the business's ability to pay, and on that criterion bargaining is clearly affordable at one fourteenth of the wage bill. The counterargument: bargaining through Selma hands the talks to a manager the union already trusts, but the owner might argue that leading the talks himself keeps control of the pay bill - the alternative route - though his own words show the talks would start badly, since he has called the workers' chosen body "outsiders". The recommendation depends on conditions: unless the owner keeps final approval of any deal Selma reaches, delegation hands away control of the pay bill; and if the union's claim rises in later years, the affordability that justifies agreement now may change.
marking_guidance: Judgement: award for a clear recommendation - recognise the union, delegate the talks with limits. Context: award for using the facts and figures - 60 workers at N$14 an hour, the N$1 claim costing N$120 000 against a N$1 680 000 wage bill. Criterion: award for naming what decides it - combined workforce strength against ability to pay. Counterargument: award for the case against delegation - the owner keeping control of the pay bill - as the alternative weighed. Condition: award for the recommendation depending on stated conditions - final approval retained, and affordability changing if claims rise.

items.prompt: Plan, without writing the full answer, a response to this 12-mark task: "Managers should keep control of every important decision rather than delegate it." Consider this view. Set out the paragraphs you would write, the judgement you would reach and the criterion that decides it, the case against your judgement, and the conditions the final recommendation would depend on.
items.canonical_answer: Plan. Paragraph 1, define the terms: delegation as the passing of authority to a subordinate with the manager still answerable; control as the manager's retained check on decisions and results. Paragraph 2, the case for the view: some decisions carry consequences too large to hand on - prices, safety, spending commitments - because the manager is the one answerable for the outcome, and an error made by an unready subordinate can reach customers before anyone above notices. Paragraph 3, the case against: keeping every decision at the top overloads managers, starves capable subordinates of development, and slows the business down, because every decision queues at one desk; the chain of command becomes a bottleneck rather than a channel. Paragraph 4, judgement: the view is right about decisions whose consequences exceed a subordinate's experience, and wrong as a general rule; the criterion is the size of the consequences together with the subordinate's readiness. Paragraph 5, conditions: the recommendation depends on whether the business trains and checks its people - delegation grows safer with training and agreed checks - and it changes if either the stakes or the staff's experience change.
marking_guidance: Judgement: the plan must state the verdict the answer would reach - right about large-consequence decisions, wrong as a general rule. Context: the plan must use facts about how delegation works - retained answerability, decisions queuing at one desk. Criterion: the plan must name what decides the verdict - the size of the consequences with the subordinate's readiness. Counterargument: the plan must include the case against the view - overload, undeveloped staff, slow decisions. Condition: the recommendation must depend on stated conditions - training and checks in place, stakes or experience changing.

items.prompt: Braga & Filhos is a family bakery in northern Portugal with 38 staff, founded by Senhor Braga, who approves every price, recipe change and shift himself; three supervisors pass his instructions to the bakers. The bakers have worked there for years and often improve recipes on their own initiative, without being asked. A supermarket chain has offered a contract that would double the bakery's output if strict daily delivery windows are met. The bakers have asked for a say in how the new volume would be scheduled, and have mentioned forming a union branch if overtime is imposed without agreement. Analyse the situation and recommend what Senhor Braga should do.
items.canonical_answer: Analysis: the structure is tall for a 38-person bakery - every decision queues at Senhor Braga - while the bakers' habit of improving recipes on their own initiative shows capability the structure leaves unused; the facts argue that the constraint on the business is the owner's approval of everything, not the staff's skill. The supermarket contract raises urgency, which is the one fact arguing for keeping command at the top. The union branch mentioned is a warning: capable staff asking for a say, and signalling they will organise if overtime is imposed without agreement. Recommendation: keep the owner's final say on prices, contract terms and food safety, but delegate the scheduling of the new volume to the supervisors and bakers as a team, meeting weekly - a broadly democratic style with autocratic control points, fitted to an experienced team under new time pressure. On the union question, the judgement is to open a regular forum with the bakers now - the say they have asked for - rather than leave them to form a branch to obtain it. The criterion that decides the style is the same as for structure: the bakers' high experience against the delivery deadlines' high urgency. The counterargument: doubling output under strict windows may seem to demand firm command, and a looser arrangement could let coordination drift - the alternative is to run the contract autocratically and accept the friction; but that would override the very people whose skill the contract depends on. The recommendation depends on conditions: if delivery windows start being missed, shift more scheduling authority back to the supervisors; unless the bakers' forum produces agreed overtime rules, the union branch will form anyway.
marking_guidance: Judgement: award for a clear recommendation - delegated scheduling under owner control, a bakers' forum opened now. Context: award for using the facts of the business - 38 staff, the owner approving everything, the bakers' initiative, the doubling contract, the union branch mentioned. Criterion: award for naming what decides the style - high staff experience against high delivery urgency. Counterargument: award for the case against - command meeting the deadlines at the cost of overriding skilled staff. Condition: award for the recommendation depending on stated conditions - missed windows returning authority, the forum needing to settle overtime rules.
